steps: Distance is the total length of the actual path travelled by an object, whereas displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from its initial to its final position in a specified direction.
If an object moves along a straight line in one direction, the magnitude of its distance and displacement are equal.
If an object changes direction or follows a curved path, the magnitude of its distance is greater than the magnitude of its displacement.
items.finalAnswer: Distance and displacement are equal in magnitude for straight-line motion in one direction; otherwise, distance is greater.

steps: Assume the bullet starts from rest and has uniform acceleration while moving through the barrel.
For motion with uniform acceleration, v² = u² + 2as. Since u = 0, a = v²/(2s).
The gun with the longer barrel produces a lower muzzle velocity, while its barrel length is greater.
Therefore, its value of v²/(2s) is smaller. The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.
items.finalAnswer: The bullet's acceleration is larger in the gun with the shorter barrel.

steps: Yes, it is possible.
A positive average velocity for the complete trip means that the net displacement is in the positive direction.
The object may move in the negative direction during part of the trip and still have a positive net displacement for the complete trip.
Therefore, its instantaneous velocity may be negative at some time during the trip.
items.finalAnswer: Yes. Instantaneous velocity can be negative during part of a trip even when average velocity for the complete trip is positive.

steps: For upward motion, take the upward direction as positive.
The ball has initial velocity +v and constant acceleration −g due to gravity.
Its velocity decreases uniformly with time, becomes zero at the highest point, and then becomes negative as the ball falls.
Thus, the correct velocity–time graph is a straight line with negative slope, starting at +v, crossing the time axis at T/2, and ending at −v at time T.
items.finalAnswer: The correct velocity–time graph is a straight line from +v at t = 0 to −v at t = T, crossing zero at T/2.

steps: The distance–time graph referred to in the question is not included, so the numerical velocities of segments a, b and c cannot be determined.
The velocity for each segment is found from the slope of that segment of the distance–time graph: velocity = change in distance / change in time.
A steeper segment represents a greater velocity; a horizontal segment represents zero velocity.
items.finalAnswer: The velocities cannot be calculated without the graph and its scale; each is the slope of its segment.

steps: Yes, it is possible for the velocity of an object to be zero at an instant while its acceleration is not zero.
For example, when a ball is thrown vertically upward, its velocity is zero for an instant at the highest point.
At that instant, its acceleration is still g downward due to gravity.
items.finalAnswer: Yes. At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball, velocity is momentarily zero but acceleration is g downward.

steps: A vector is represented graphically by a directed line segment.
The length of the line segment, drawn according to a suitable scale, represents the magnitude of the vector.
The arrowhead shows the direction of the vector.
The vector is labelled with its symbol.
items.finalAnswer: A vector is shown by a scaled directed line segment: its length represents magnitude and its arrowhead represents direction.

steps: Rest: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings.
Motion: An object is in motion if its position changes with time relative to its surroundings.
Rest and motion are relative terms; an object may be at rest relative to one body and in motion relative to another.
items.finalAnswer: An object is at rest if its position does not change with time relative to its surroundings, and in motion if it does.
